rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-ʿAṭāʾ reports Ibn ʿAbbās glossing the purified person as one who professes that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (من قال لا إله إلا الله)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī gives a similar gloss: the purified person professes that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: لا إله إلا الله) (¬1). ونحو ذلك قال الكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification means cleansing oneself of sins through obedience instead of becoming sullied by disobedience, seeking to be virtuous in goodness.
rows.anchor: {تزكى} تطهير من الذنوب بالطاعة بدلا من التدنس بالمعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is exalted above the heretics' denial and is free of the attributes the polytheists ascribe to Him.
rows.anchor: جل عن إلحاد الملحدين، ونزه عما يقول المشركون في صفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, God deserves incomparable praise: He is more powerful and knowing than any other, while every other possessor of power depends on Him and He depends on none.
rows.anchor: أقدر من كل قادر، وأعلم من كل عالم، وقادر سواه محتاج إليه وهو غني عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the King is the one in whose hand lie reward and punishment; the author explains that He owns them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد الذي بيده الثواب والعقاب)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥaqq here means the possessor of truth or right; the author says he discussed this earlier.
rows.anchor: {الحق} معناه: ذو الحق، وقد مر وتقدم الكلام فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In reports through ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Ṣāliḥ, Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet began reciting before Gabriel finished, eager to retain the revelation and afraid it would slip from memory, so God forbade this.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء وأبي صالح: (كان النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- يبادر جبريل فيقرأ

words: وَلَا تَعْجَلْ بِٱلْقُرْءَانِ مِن قَبْلِ أَن يُقْضَىٰٓ إِلَيْكَ وَحْيُهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command means do not recite until Gabriel has completed reciting the revelation to you.
rows.anchor: {ولا تعجل بالقرآن} أي: بقراءته {من قبل أن يقضى إليك وحيه}

words: مِن قَبْلِ أَن يُقْضَىٰٓ إِلَيْكَ وَحْيُهُۥ
rows.speaker: المفضل
rows.claim: Al-Mufaḍḍal interprets the phrase as before the revelation is fully delivered and completed.
rows.anchor: وقال المفضل: (من قبل أن يوفى ويتمم)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the Prophet strained to memorize every revelation before Gabriel departed, fearing he would forget it; this verse was then sent down.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (كان رسول الله -صلى الله عليه وسلم- إذا نزل عليه جبريل بالقرآن أتعب نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author links the command to 75:16 and notes that al-Kalbī holds this recitation interpretation while al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba choose it.
rows.anchor: وهذا كقوله: {لا تحرك به لسانك لتعجل به}

rows.speaker: مجاهد، قتادة
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda understand the command as not reciting a newly revealed verse to anyone until God makes it clear; the author says this bars recitation and dictation before its meaning is clear.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وقتادة: (لا تتله على أحد حتى نبينه لك)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭiyya's report, Ibn ʿAbbās says not to convey the Qurʾān to people before the explanation of its interpretation comes.
rows.anchor: رواية عطية عن ابن عباس قال: (لا تلقه إلى الناس قبل أن يأتيك بيان تأويله)

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the verse to forbid asking for the Qurʾān's revelation before its revelation arrives.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض أهل التفسير أن معنى هذه الآية: (لا تسأل إنزال القرآن من قبل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports that a man struck his wife, she sought retaliation, and the Prophet initially ruled for retaliation before this verse came and he paused until 4:34 was revealed.
rows.anchor: وروى جرير (¬3) عن الحسن في سبب نزول هذه الآية: (أن رجلا لطم امرأته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the claim that the verse was revealed about that incident: the story does not bear on it, apart from its final command to seek increased knowledge; the retaliation ruling was superseded by 4:34.
rows.anchor: ولا تعلق لهذه الآية في القصة التي ذكرها الحسن حتى يقال إنها نازلة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God commands the Prophet to ask for more knowledge: teach me what I do not know.
rows.anchor: بأن يسأل الله تعالى زيادة علم، والمعنى: علمني ما لا أعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's covenant with Adam means that He commanded and enjoined him.
rows.anchor: {ولقد عهدنا إلى آدم} أي: أمرناه وأوصينا إليه

rows.speaker: الكلبي، السدي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and al-Suddī say Adam was charged not to eat from the tree.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي والسدي: (عهدنا إليه ألا يأكل من الشجرة)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Adam was told not to approach the tree.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: (ألا يقرب الشجرة)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī takes “before” to mean before Adam ate from the tree.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (من قبل أن يأكل من الشجرة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading takes “before” as before the people who broke God's covenant and abandoned faith; these are the people mentioned in 20:113, and Adam too had been covenanted with.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: (من قبل هؤلاء الذين فقضوا عهدي وتركوا الإيمان بي)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses Adam's forgetting as abandoning God's covenant.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (فترك عهدي)

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Adam left undone what he had been commanded.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: (ترك ما أمر به)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī interprets the forgetting as abandoning God's covenant.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (ترك عهدنا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says all the reported views agree that nasiya here means “left” or “abandoned.”
rows.anchor: هذا قول الجميع في أن نسي هاهنا: ترك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says “he forgot” means “he left,” since one is not held accountable for forgetting.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ({فنسي} هاهنا فترك؛ لأن الناسي لا يؤاخذ بنسيانه)

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd reads this as literal forgetting, but the author rejects that: forgetfulness is not accountable, and Satan reminded Adam and Eve of the prohibition in 7:20.
rows.anchor: وحمل ابن زيد النسيان هاهنا على الذي هو ضد الذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAzm is a firm resolve of the heart to do something and the self's firm commitment to act.
rows.anchor: معنى العزم: عقد القلب على أمر يفعله، وهو توطين النفس على الفعل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, Ibn ʿAbbās takes the phrase to mean that Adam lacked patience to refrain from eating the tree.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (يريد صبرا عن أكل الشجرة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam did not persevere in the resolve he had made to avoid what he was forbidden to eat.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنه لم يصبر على ما وطن عليه نفسه من ترك ما نهي عن أكله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan likewise glosses the phrase as lacking patience concerning what Adam was forbidden.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول الحسن: (صبرا عما نهي عنه)

rows.speaker: عطية العوفي
rows.claim: ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī explains it as not holding to what God had entrusted him with regarding the command.
rows.anchor: وقال عطية العوفي: (عن ما حفظنا لما أمر به)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī interprets the lack of resolve as lack of patience in the face of sins.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (صبرا على الذنوب)

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسلم
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim takes ʿazm as a firmly held judgment or decision.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن مسلم: (رأيا معزوما عليه)

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An unattributed view takes it as a firm commitment, which Adam failed to keep when he obeyed his envious enemy Iblīs, who refused to prostrate to him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: (عقدا ثابتا حيث أطاع عدوه إبليس الذي حسده وأبى أن يسجد له)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, Ibn ʿAbbās says the hardship is the toil and distress of worldly life.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (يريد شقاء الدنيا ونصبها)

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan also understands worldly hardship, observing that Adam's descendants are all laboring and miserable.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: (عني به شقاء الدنيا، ألا ترى ابن آدم إلا ناصبا شقيا)

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reports that Adam was sent down a red bull to work with, and had to wipe sweat from his brow; this was his hardship.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: (أهبط إلى آدم ثورا أحمر كان يعتمل عليه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī specifies the labor as plowing, planting, kneading dough, and baking bread.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (الحرث والزرع والعجن والخبر)

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī glosses the hardship as the toil of earning a livelihood.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن علي: (فتشقى في كد المعيشة)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the singular verb instead of a dual as addressing Adam, whose action stands for his wife's; singular address also suits the verse endings, like the singular sitter for the two sides in 50:17.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (ولم يقل: فتشقيا، لأن آدم المخاطب وفي فعله اكتفاء من فعل المرأة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction places the clause of not being hungry in the accusative as though governed by an implicit أن, as in “you have property.”
rows.anchor: {إن} في موضع نصب بأن، كما تقول: إن لك مالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not being hungry means having satiety and clothing in Paradise.
rows.anchor: {ألا تجوع} بمعنى الشبع، كأنه قيل: إن لك الشبع فيها والاكتساء

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the clothing is made from the bull's hide.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (من لباس الثور)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Adam would remain free of hunger for as long as he stayed in Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد أن لك ما دمت في الجنة ألا تجوع فيها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author gives the Arabic forms for being unclothed: ʿariya, yaʿrā, ʿuryan, ʿārin, and feminine ʿuryāna or ʿariyya.
rows.anchor: يقال: عري فلان من ثوبه يعرى عريا فهو عار وعريان، والأنثى عريانة وعرية

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith reports that the Prophet rode Abū Ṭalḥa's horse ʿaryan, without a saddle.
rows.anchor: ومنه الحديث: (أن # النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- ركب فرسا

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī says Arabs call a horse ʿarī and horses aʿrāʾ, but do not use ʿarī for a man.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري: (والعرب تقول: فرس عري. وخيل أعراء ولا يقال رجل عري)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says wa-annaka is accusative, coordinated with allā tajūʿa; it may also be nominative because the sense is “you do not thirst,” explaining the clause after inna.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: {وأنك} في موضع نصب نسقا على قوله: {ألا تجوع} ويجوز أن تكون في موضع رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with kasra, wa-innaka, begins a new clause coordinated with the preceding sentence.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ: وإنك بالكسر على الاستئناف، وعطف جملة كلام على جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍaḥā means that a person is exposed to the sun and its heat.
rows.anchor: يقال: ضحا الرجل إذا برز للشمس فأصابه حرها

rows.speaker: النضر
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr gives the form ḍaḥā li-l-shams, yaḍḥā, ḍaḥwan.
rows.anchor: وقال النضر: (ضحا للشمس يضحى

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives the forms ḍaḥaytu li-l-shams and ḍaḥītu, both with the imperfect aḍḥā.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: (ضحيت للشمس، وضحيت، أضحى منهما جميعا)

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammar reports the forms ḍaḥiya/yaḍḥā, ḍaḥyan, ḍaḥā/yaḍḥū, and ḍaḥwan.
rows.anchor: وحكى شمر: (ضحي، يضحى، ضحيا، وضحا، يضحو، ضحوا)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj cites a line about a man who is exposed to the sun at midday and becomes chilled by evening; it illustrates yaḍḥā.
rows.anchor: وأنشد الزجاج (¬4): رأت رجلا أما إذا الشمس عارضت ... فيضحى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Ḍaḥḥāk's report, Ibn ʿAbbās says Adam would not suffer thirst or heat as people do in this world.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية الضحاك يقول: (لا تعطش فيها كما يعطش أهل الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿIkrima's report, Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the phrase as not being struck by the sun.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية عكرمة: (لا تصيبك الشمس)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In reports through al-Wālibī and ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās says there is neither heat nor thirst in Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية الوالبي، وعطاء: (لا يصيبك فيها حر ولا عطش)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam is not exposed to the sun's harmful heat; Paradise has no sun, only extended shade.
rows.anchor: ليس في الجنة شمس إنما هو ظل ممدود

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the two commanded to descend as Adam and Iblīs.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد آدم وإبليس)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this verse is explained in Sūrat al-Baqara, referring to the parallel account of Adam's descent and guidance.
rows.anchor: والآية مفسرة في سورة البقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author assigns “does not go astray” to this world and “does not suffer” to the next life.
rows.anchor: {فلا يضل} أي: في الدنيا (ولا يشقى) [في الآخرة.

words: فَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَ هُدَاىَ فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God protects the follower of the Qurʾān from error in this world and misery in the next, quoting the verse.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (أجار الله تابع القرآن من أن يضل في الدنيا أو يشقى في الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses God's reminder as His admonition.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد عن موعظتي)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī interprets it as the Qurʾān, which the person neither believes nor follows.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (عن القرآن فلم يؤمن به ولم يتبعه)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍank means constriction and distress; anything constricted can be called ḍank, as in a constricted house or life, and the word is used for constricted living.
rows.anchor: الضنك أصله في اللغة: الضيق والشدة، وكل ما ضاق فهو ضنك يقال: منزل ضنك

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites ʿAntara's verse about death appearing when people settle in a constricted dwelling to attest the sense of ḍank.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو عبيدة قول عنترة (¬7): إن المنية لو تمثل مثلت ... مثلي إذا نزلوا بضنك المنزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A large-bodied woman is called ḍanāk because her skin is tight over her flesh; ḍank is originally a verbal noun then used adjectivally, explaining the feminine form maʿīshatan ḍankā.
rows.anchor: ومنه قيل للمرأة الضخمة الكثيرة اللحم: ضناك؛ لأن جلدها قد ضاق بلحمها

rows.speaker: النبي، أبو هريرة، أبو سعيد الخدري، ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The most common exegetical view, attributed to the Prophet and to Abū Hurayra, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and Ibn Masʿūd, is that the constricted life is punishment in the grave.
rows.anchor: وأكثر ما جاء في التفسير المعيشة الضنك: (أنه عذاب القبر) عن النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم-، وعن أبي هريرة

rows.speaker: الحسن، الكلبي، ابن زيد، قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, al-Kalbī, Ibn Zayd, and Qatāda interpret the constricted life as punishment in the Fire, including food of zaqqūm, ghislīn, and ḍarīʿ.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن، والكلبي، وابن زيد، وقتادة: (هو عذاب النار، وأكل الزقوم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, Ibn ʿAbbās specifies the punishment of the grave as its squeeze until the ribs are displaced.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (يريد: ضغطة القبر حتى تختلف أضلاعه)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Wālibī's report, Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as the wretched or miserable person.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (يريد: ضغطة القبر حتى تختلف أضلاعه) (¬1). وقال في رواية الوالبي: (الشقي)

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the person will be blind in his eyesight.
rows.anchor: قيل في التفسير: (أعمى البصر)

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that he will be blind to proof or argument.
rows.anchor: وقيل: (أعمى الحجة)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains that the person has no proof to guide him, or has proof but is blinded to it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (وتأويله أنه لا حجة له يهتدي إليها، أن له حجة

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another scholar says that when blindness is unqualified, its apparent sense is blindness of sight; the following passage supports this view, though the excerpt breaks off before completing the evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: (العمى إذا أطلق كان الظاهر عمى البصر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author questions the interpretation “blind to my proof”: he cannot see how a disbeliever could have been clear-sighted about proof when he had no proof in either world.
rows.anchor: {قال رب لم حشرتني أعمى} عن حجتي {وقد كنت بصيرا} بها في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answers the disbeliever: this is how things are, as you now see.
rows.anchor: قال الله مجيبا لهذا الكافر كذلك الأمر كما ترى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الكلبي، أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī, and the exegetes say the person abandoned God's signs and did not believe; correspondingly, he is left in the Fire today.
rows.anchor: هذا قول ابن عباس، والكلبي، وأهل التفسير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “whoever acted extravagantly” as one who committed shirk.
rows.anchor: {وكذلك} كما ذكرنا {نجزي من أسرف} قال ابن عباس: (أشرك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hereafter's punishment is more awful and greater than the grave punishment just mentioned; this supports reading the constricted life as punishment of the grave.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدلس على أن المراد بقوله: {معيشة ضنكا}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They” refers to the polytheists.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {وقالوا} يعني المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They demand that Muḥammad bring a sign from his Lord like those given to earlier prophets, such as the she-camel or the staff.
rows.anchor: هلا يأتينا محمد بآية من ربه كما أتى بها الأنبياء نحو الناقة والعصا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says signs had already come to them, but they demanded signs of their own choosing.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (وقد أتتهم الآيات ولكنهم طلبوا أن يأتيهم ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān clarifies the Torah, Gospel, and earlier scriptures and is a greater sign, since an unlettered Prophet reported their contents without reading them, as the People of the Book attest; this is al-Kalbī's view and that of others.
rows.anchor: وذلك أعظم آية إذ أخبر أمي بما فيها من غير قراءة كتاب على ما تصدقه أهل الكتب

rows.speaker: قول آخر
rows.claim: Another view says the Qurʾān warns through accounts of earlier peoples destroyed after demanding and rejecting signs, raising the question why these people would respond differently.
rows.anchor: وفيه قول آخر وهو: (أن المعنى أولم تأتهم ببيان ما في الكتب من أنباء الأمم

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Some exegetes understand the proof in the earlier scriptures as their glad tidings of Muḥammad and descriptions of his qualities.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل التفسير: {بينة ما في الصحف الأولى} ما تقدم من البشارة بمحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Each” means both sides: the Muslims wait for God's promise concerning the opponents, while the opponents await calamity that would let them be rid of the Muslims; “wait” means await.
rows.anchor: منكم {متربص} مهو نحن نتربص بكم وعدا لنا فيكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the even path as the upright religion.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد الدين المستقيم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is which of the two sides is guided away from error: “we or you?”
rows.anchor: من الضلالة أنحن أم أنتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqf means a house's roof; the sky is to the earth as a roof is to a house, and is named the raised roof in 52:5.
rows.anchor: والسماء للأرض كالسقف للبيت، فجعلت السماء سقفا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الكلبي، الفراء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the sky is guarded from devils by stars; al-Kalbī agrees and al-Farrāʾ chooses this interpretation, supported by 15:17.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: من الشياطين بالنجوم

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq offers another interpretation: God preserves the sky from falling to earth except by His permission, as 22:65 says.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو إسحاق وجها آخر قال: حفظه الله من الوقوع على الأرض إلا بإذنه

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another scholar says the sky is preserved from collapse and from the long-term deterioration that affects ordinary roofs.
rows.anchor: وزاد غيره: محفوظا من الهدم، ومن أن يلحقها ما يلحق غيرها من السقوف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses the preserved roof as raised.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: {سقفا محفوظا} مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says “raised” conveys the sense rather than a direct gloss: its height preserves the sky because no one can reach it by demolition or artifice.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى وليس بتفسير. وذلك أنه مرفوع رفعا لا يطمع أحد أن يناله بنقض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies “they” as the polytheists.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد المشركين

rows.speaker: الكلبي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and other exegetes identify the sky's signs as its sun, moon, and stars.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي وغيره من المفسرين: شمسها وقمرها ونجومها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists turn away by failing to contemplate and reflect on these signs, which would show them that their Creator has no partner.
rows.anchor: لا يتدبرونها، ولا يتفكرون فيها، فيعلموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “All” refers to all the heavenly bodies that rise.
rows.anchor: {كل} يعني الطوالع كلها

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says falak in the hadith usage is the rotation of the sky, specifically the act of revolving.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: الفلك في الحديث (¬6) دوران (¬7) السماء

rows.speaker: المنجمون
rows.claim: Astronomers describe seven spheres below the sky, each carrying one of the seven planets at a different height, revolving by God's permission.
rows.anchor: وأما المنجمون فيقولون: سبعة أطواق (¬1) دون السماء قد ركبت فيها النجوم السبعة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة، الأصمعي
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda transmits from al-Aṣmaʿī that a falak can be a round, raised part of the land, singular falaka; al-Rāʿī's line describes the resulting raised circular form.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو عبيدة عن الأصمعي: الفلك: قطع من الأرض تستدير وترتفع عما حولها

rows.speaker: الراعي
rows.claim: Al-Rāʿī's line uses falak muzhar for a rounded rise that appears when lowlands and valleys are feared or exposed.
rows.anchor: قال الراعي: إذا جفن هول بطون (¬5) البلاد ... تضمنها فلك مزهر (¬6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, falak can mean anything round; its plural is aflāk, as in a spindle whorl and the rounded shape of a girl's breast.
rows.anchor: والفلك في كلام العرب: كل شيء مستدير، وجمعه أفلاك، ومنه فلكة المغزل

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says falak means an orbit and a circular path.
rows.anchor: وأما المفسرون، فقال السدي في قوله

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says falak is the sky's roundness and, by extension, any circular thing; the stars turn within the round sky.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: الفلك استدارة السماء، وكل شيء استدار فهو فلك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid compares the orbit to the shape of a millstone; the author explains that stars circle the pole as a millstone turns around its iron spindle.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول مجاهد: كهيئة حديدة الرحى

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes say the falak is the circular track that contains the stars.
rows.anchor: وعلى (¬9) هذا معنى قول أكثر المفسرين، قالوا: الفلك مدار النجوم الذي يضمها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan compares the falak to a mill or a spindle whorl, meaning a rounded track in which the stars run.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الفلك طاحونة [كهيئة فلكة المغزل

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the falak is between heaven and earth and consists of the paths of the stars, sun, and moon, like the astronomers' spheres.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: الفلك الذي بين السماء والأرض [من] (¬3) مجاري النجوم والشمس والقمر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says falak is the pole around which the stars revolve, but the author rejects this: the word must name the circular container in which they swim.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الفلك: القطب الذي تدور به النجوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yasbaḥūn means they move swiftly like swimmers; the verb can also describe a horse extending its forelegs in a run, as in al-Aʿshā's verse, and 79:3 calls stars swimmers.
rows.anchor: أي: يجرون بسرعة كالسابح في الماء، وقد قال في موضع آخر في صفة النجوم: {والسابحات سبحا}

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line “a swift, spirited horse” illustrates calling a running horse a swimmer.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الأعشى: وسابح ذي ميعة (¬1) ضامر (¬2)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Some assumed swimming only applies in water and therefore made the falak a water wave for stars; al-Farrāʾ reports this view, which the author calls mistaken.
rows.anchor: وحكى الفراء هذا القول في

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق، أبو عبيدة، الفراء، المبرد
rows.claim: The masculine rational plural is used because these bodies are described with a rational action; Abū Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayda, al-Farrāʾ, al-Mubarrad, and linguists cite akalūnī al-barāghīth; the line of al-Jaʿdī and 12:4 illustrate the construction.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحق: قيل {يسبحون} هو كما يقال لما يعقل

rows.speaker: الجعدي
rows.claim: Al-Jaʿdī's line illustrates the plural verb marking in the expression “the stars of the Great Bear drew near and descended.”
rows.anchor: وأنشد للجعدي: تمرزتها والديك يدعو صباحه ... إذا ما بنو نعش دنوا فتصوبوا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says idols neither provide nor give anything, and if people do not worship them they cause no harm.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: يقول لا يرزقكم ولا يعطيكم شيئا

words: مَا لَا يَنفَعُكُمْ شَيْـًۭٔا وَلَا يَضُرُّكُمْ
rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says idols do no good when worshiped and no harm when abandoned.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول الكلبي: لا ينفعكم إن عبدتموه ولا يضركم إن تركتموه

words: مَا لَا يَنفَعُكُمْ شَيْـًۭٔا وَلَا يَضُرُّكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the admission made the proof decisive, Abraham rebukes them; the argument urges worship of God, who controls benefit through reward for worship and harm through punishment for failing to worship.
rows.anchor: فلما اتجهت الحجة عليهم بإقرارهم وبخهم إبراهيم فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The man of the whale” is Jonah ibn Mattā; God named him for being held in the whale's belly, as another verse calls him the companion of the fish.
rows.anchor: وهو يونس بن متى (¬6) سماه الله تعالى ذا النون لما حبسه في بطن النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supplies an implied command: “And remember the man of the whale.”
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {وذا النون} أي: واذكر ذا النون

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says Jonah went away angry with his people.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: مغاضبا لقومه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-ʿAwfī's report, Ibn ʿAbbās says the Israelites pressed Jonah to ask a conquering king to release their captives; after asking the prophet Shuʿyāʾ whether God had ordered or named him, Jonah left angry at Shuʿyāʾ, the king, and his people.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس في رواية العوفي، قال: إن شعيا (¬2) النبي والملك الذي كان في وقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that account, Jonah was punished for leaving what Shuʿyāʾ and the people had ordered, since the Qurʾān says the whale swallowed him while he was blameworthy.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا عوقب بتركه ما أمره به شعيا وقومه لأن الله تعالى قال فيه: {فالتقمه الحوت وهو مليم}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن مسعود، سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Another view says Jonah went away angry with his Lord; this is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Masʿūd, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: إنه ذهب مغاضبا لربه. وهذا قول ابن عباس في رواية عطاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Jonah had warned his people of punishment and left; after God lifted it, Jonah heard and fled toward a loaded ship.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لما وعد قومه العذاب، وخرج من بينهم، ورفع عنهم العذاب

rows.speaker: مسروق عن عبد الله
rows.claim: Masrūq reports from ʿAbd Allāh the gloss “a servant who fled from his Lord.”
rows.anchor: وروى مسروق عن عبد الله في قوله: {إذ ذهب مغاضبا} قال: عبد أبق من ربه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير، الحسن
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Jonah went angry with his Lord, and al-Ḥasan gives a similar view.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: ذهب مغاضبا لربه (¬2). ونحو هذا قال الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba argues that people recoil from attributing sins to prophets and distort scripture to avoid it; he cites a report that prophets erred except Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā, and points to Joseph's admission in 12:53.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذه الطريقة مال ابن قتيبة، فإنه يقول في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: الحديث
rows.claim: A report Ibn Qutayba cites says every prophet erred and intended a sin except Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā.
rows.anchor: [روي في الحديث: أنه] (¬5) ليس من نبي إلا (¬6) وقد أخطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author invokes Joseph's “I do not acquit myself” and his soul's urging toward evil as a comparison; Ibn Qutayba reads this as inward thought when desire arose.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال (¬1) يوسف عليه السلام: {وما أبرئ نفسي إن النفس لأمارة بالسوء}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author asks what fault would merit the whale and confinement if Jonah merely grew angry with his people; “blameworthy” means he committed an offense deserving blame.
rows.anchor: وما الأمر الذي ألام فيه؟

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that after Jonah left the whale, God gave him a gourd tree for shade; when it dried Jonah wept, and God reminded him that he had wanted more than 100,000 people destroyed and ordered him back to his people.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن ابن عباس في قصته: أنه لما خرج من بطن الحوت أنبت الله له شجرة من يقطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This shows Jonah desired punishment for his people and resented its being lifted; sailing away disobeyed God's order that he return to them.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أنه اشتهى نزول عذاب الله بقومه، وكره دفعه عنهم، وأن ركوبه البحر كان معصية لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects saying Jonah was angry with God, calling that a grave claim that cannot be made about prophets.
rows.anchor: فأما أن يقال إنه غاضب ربه، فهم عظيم، ولا يجوز القول بذلك في الأنبياء

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba chooses to read mughāḍiban as resentful or affronted: Jonah left upset that his warning of punishment had not come true and feared being seen as a liar.
rows.anchor: وروي وجه آخر من التأويل في قوله: {إذ ذهب مغاضبا} وهو أن

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ reports that a king ordered Jonah, at Shuʿyāʾ's direction, to go to Nineveh; Jonah resented being sent by anyone but God, was swallowed, and was then sent to preach to the people, who believed.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أبي صالح: أن ملكا من ملوك بني إسرائيل كان أمره بالمسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Abū Ṣāliḥ's account, Jonah's resentment occurred before his mission.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا مغاضبته كانت قبل رسالته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the repeatedly transmitted account that Jonah's departure followed his mission and God's lifting the impending punishment; Jonah resented the reprieve and feared appearing to have lied, so he fled aboard the loaded ship.
rows.anchor: ولكن الصحيح الذي تواترت به الرواية
